The study was approved by the local ethics committee at UCL Speech, Hearing and Phonetic Sciences (SHaPS-2023-CM-038), and all participants provided informed consent prior to completing the experiment.
Four hundred participants were recruited via the online recruitment platform Prolific.ac.

Participants were invited to the study based on the following inclusion criteria: aged between 18-50 years old, with English as their first language, having spent of their time in the UK before turning 18, and without hearing difficulties or dyslexia.
We further required that participants had a minimum approval rating of 95% on Prolific and a minimum of 10 previous submissions on the platform.
These participants were removed with replacement.
Five additional participants were removed for choosing to wait on all 4 trials of the willingness-to-wait paradigm (following Bains et al., 2023).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori sample size calculation in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009) used the observed effect size of 0.208 (based on the within-participants effect of Pleasantness on Enjoyment in Experiment 2 of McGettigan et al., 2026) with an alpha of 0.05 and power of 0.8. This suggested a total sample of N=184 participants. A larger target sample of 400 was however chosen to match the total number of trials (i.e. observations) in Experiment 2 of McGettigan et al., (2026), which was 1600 (N=80 participants x 10 trials x 2 repeated-measures conditions).

live_data_statements: Four hundred participants were recruited via the online recruitment platform Prolific.ac.

Participants were invited to the study based on the following inclusion criteria: aged between 18-50 years old, with English as their first language, having spent of their time in the UK before turning 18, and without hearing difficulties or dyslexia.
We further required that participants had a minimum approval rating of 95% on Prolific and a minimum of 10 previous submissions on the platform.
These participants were removed with replacement.
Five additional participants were removed for choosing to wait on all 4 trials of the willingness-to-wait paradigm (following Bains et al., 2023).

The study was approved by the local ethics committee at UCL Speech, Hearing and Phonetic Sciences (SHaPS-2023-CM-038), and all participants provided informed consent prior to completing the experiment.
Having read each extract, participants provided ratings of the imagined narrator's gender (on a 0-100 scale from "very masculine male" to "very feminine female") and age (from 0-100 years old).

The experimental trials were interspersed with 2 vigilance trials in fixed positions (after the 1 st and 3 rd experimental trials), in which the participants were required to choose the number stated by a synthetic voice (1 female-sounding, 1 male-sounding; both distinct from the main trial narrator voices).

Participants recruited from Prolific were directed to the experiment on Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020) where they read the study information sheet and provided informed consent.
After all 4 trials, participants were presented again with the first excerpt from each of the 4 books.

After rating suitability for all 4 stories, the participants were asked which of the 2 narrator voices sounded more pleasant to them, with the response options "male voice", "female voice", and "no preference".
Participants were then invited to, if relevant, report any technical difficulties and make further comments about the experiment.

text.text: While a reader might imagine the narrator's and characters' voices in a written book, a spoken narrative solidifies the relationship between the narrator and the text.
Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects narrative listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes.
In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four spoken narratives in a willingness-to-wait paradigm.
We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately.

However, we observed a dissociation in the observed effects of perceived narrator-to-story fit: specifically, higher individual evaluations significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening.
This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting narrative listening enjoyment.

Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants' enjoyment of spoken narratives is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by withinor between-group aggregate ratings.
Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of narration as a way to promote enjoyment of spoken narratives and, potentially, audiobooks.

Book language typically features more advanced vocabulary and greater syntactic complexity, and exposure to books supports the development of both linguistic and non-linguistic abilities, including skills such as emotion processing and theory of mind (Nation et al., 2022).

text.text: Yet, recent years have seen a decline in the levels of reading for pleasure, with large proportions of children and adults who do not consider themselves to be readers (Bone et al., 2025; Clark et al., 2025; Cremin & Scholes, 2024; Spaulding et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Yet, recent years have seen a decline in the levels of reading for pleasure, with large proportions of children and adults who do not consider themselves to be readers <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bone et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Clark et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Cremin & Scholes, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Spaulding et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This presents the risk that large and increasing proportions of people are missing out on the benefits of engaging with books.

Recent findings have underlined the importance of reward systems for engaging with the benefits of book language, by showing that greater enjoyment of a written or audio book excerpt predicts both increased comprehension of the book, and a greater motivation to continue reading or listening to it (Bains et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2025; McGettigan et al., 2026).

text.text: This motivates a need to investigate the factors that might enhance enjoyment, as potential levers for promoting cognitive engagement with books.
Audiobooks offer an alternative to book reading, while preserving access to the language of written books.
A crucial distinction between written and spoken versions of narratives is that while the written form leaves the narrator's voice to the reader's imagination, an audiobook defines it.

This opens up the possibility to use audio design as a lever to enhance enjoyment and engagement: Previous work has shown that greater narrator pleasantness and familiarity are both associated with increased enjoyment of spoken narratives (McGettigan et al., 2026), and other work has shown that acoustic features of narration (such as speaking rate) can predict narrative absorption (Lange et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This opens up the possibility to use audio design as a lever to enhance enjoyment and engagement: Previous work has shown that greater narrator pleasantness and familiarity are both associated with increased enjoyment of spoken narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(McGettigan et al., 2026)</ref>, and other work has shown that acoustic features of narration (such as speaking rate) can predict narrative absorption <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Lange et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, less is known about how the relationship between a voice and the specific text it is narrating -or the narrator-to-story "fit"might impact the listening experience as well as related outcomes such as comprehension.

The current study aimed to investigate this by measuring how variation in narrator-to-story fit impacted listening enjoyment, comprehension, and motivation to continue listening (measured as willingness to wait).

There are several ways in which a heard narration might be perceived to match or mismatch with the linguistic content of a narrative, in terms of both the speaker's perceived person characteristics (e.g. age, sex/gender, personality traits, first language / nationality, social class) and/or their delivery style (e.g. speaking rate, voice quality, affective prosody).
However, voice gender presents itself as the strongest candidate for a first investigation of narrator-to-story fit.

As a speaker property, binary sex judgements from adult voices can be performed with high accuracy and from very brief exposures (Owren et al., 2007), due to the substantial sexual dimorphism in human voice fundamental frequency (related to pitch) and formant frequences (related to timbre or vocal size); acoustic variations within male and female voices further give rise to stereotyped inferences about speakers that are at least partly mediated by percepts of relative masculinity and femininity (Ko et al., 2006).

text.text: Gender also has arguably the largest existing evidence base in relation to the interaction of (perceived) voice properties with cognitive and linguistic processes.

For example, in an auditory version of the Stroop effect, listeners were slower to label the gender of a female speaker speaking the word "father" (incongruent) than "mother" (congruent) or "person" (neutral) (Sommers & Danielson, 1999).

text.text: Similarly, the processing of grammatical gender of spoken words is primed by congruence in the sex of the speaker (Casado et al., 2023).

text.text: Other work has shown that the congruence between the gender of a talker's voice and the gender stereotypicality of their utterance modulated P600 evoked responses, indicative of impacts on the integration of speaker properties with sentence meaning and stereotypical beliefs (Lattner & Friederici, 2003).

text.text: In the current study we therefore sought to manipulate narrator-to-story fit via the correspondence between the expected gender of an audiobook narration and its actual heard narration.

To do this, we first ran a pilot study in which we obtained ratings for the expected gender of the "ideal narrator" of twenty book extracts, and from these selected examples yielding strong expectations of either a male or a female narrator voice.

In a first main experiment (Experiment 1), these stories were combined with either a male or a female voice to generate gender-congruent and gender-incongruent narrations for a willingness-to-wait paradigm that measured reward as self-rated enjoyment of the narrative and motivation as the decision to wait (or not) in order to hear more of the narrative.

Finding that the categorical gender congruence manipulation in Experiment 1 was a less effective predictor of listening enjoyment than individual evaluations of narrator-to-story fit, we ran a second experiment (Experiment 2) to further investigate fit ratings as a predictor of enjoyment, comparing the predictive power of within-participant (i.e. trialwise), within-group, and between-group estimates.

This study tested whether a categorical manipulation of congruence between the gender of a narrator and the linguistic content of the story being narrated could modulate the experiences and outcomes of listening, using a willingness-to-wait task.
Four hundred participants were recruited via the online recruitment platform Prolific.ac.

Participants were invited to the study based on the following inclusion criteria: aged between 18-50 years old, with English as their first language, having spent of their time in the UK before turning 18, and without hearing difficulties or dyslexia.
We further required that participants had a minimum approval rating of 95% on Prolific and a minimum of 10 previous submissions on the platform.

An a priori sample size calculation in G*Power (Faul et al., 2009) used the observed effect size of 0.208 (based on the within-participants effect of Pleasantness on Enjoyment in Experiment 2 of McGettigan et al., 2026) with an alpha of 0.05 and power of 0.8.

A larger target sample of 400 was however chosen to match the total number of trials (i.e. observations) in Experiment 2 of McGettigan et al., (2026), which was 1600 (N=80 participants x 10 trials x 2 repeated-measures conditions).

Three participants asked for their data to be removed from the analysis, in response to a debrief question inviting participants to report honestly (and without penalty) if they had not completed the tasks properly in line with the instructions.

8.4 years)), all of whom passed the in-task vigilance checks.

The study was approved by the local ethics committee at UCL Speech, Hearing and Phonetic Sciences (SHaPS-2023-CM-038), and all participants provided informed consent prior to completing the experiment.
All participants who completed the experiment were rewarded £2.25.

The stimuli comprised 8 spoken narrative excerpts (2 sequential excerpts from each of 4 books), which were generated from texts used in Jones et al. (2025).
text.formatted: The stimuli comprised 8 spoken narrative excerpts (2 sequential excerpts from each of 4 books), which were generated from texts used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Jones et al. (2025)</ref>.

text.text: The 4 chosen books were selected using a pilot study, in which 40 adult participants (16 female, 24 male, Mean age 36.0 years (s.d.
7.3 years), recruited using the same inclusion criteria as above, were asked to read the text of the first excerpt from 20 different books and instructed to imagine the ideal narrator for each text.
Having read each extract, participants provided ratings of the imagined narrator's gender (on a 0-100 scale from "very masculine male" to "very feminine female") and age (from 0-100 years old).

They also rated each extract for how much they enjoyed it (from1 = not at all to9 = extremely) and how likely they would be to buy the book from which the extract was taken (from1 = not at all to9 = extremely).

Using the gender rating data, 2 female-expected and 2 male-expected excerpts were chosen whose ideal narrators yielded gender scores that were significantly lower (male) or higher (female) than the scale midpoint (50): the selections were validated via significant two-tailed one-sample t-tests, which confirmed large effect sizes (Cohen's d > 0.8) for all selected stories.

text.text: Further constraints on selection were that the mean expected age of the narrators should be relatively similar across all 4 books (to mitigate against age (in)congruence as a confound with the manipulation of interest), and that they should produce relatively similar mean enjoyment and purchase likelihood ratings.
See Table 1 for details of the final selections.

text.text: Each pair of book excerpts was sequential, such that the second excerpt could be presented in trials where the participant chose to wait to hear more of a given book.
Comprehension questions accompanying each audiobook in Experiment 1 were the same as those used in Jones et al. (2025).

text.text: Spoken audio versions of each book excerpt were produced as one WAV file per excerpt, using text-to-speech synthesis in ElevenLabs (elevenlabs.io).

One female-sounding voice identity ("Elizabeth -Professional British Narrator") and one male-sounding voice identity ("Christopher -Smooth, calm, and very English") were selected from voices that were available via ElevenLabs for community use.

Both synthetic voices had been created using ElevenLabs' Professional Voice Clone tool, which produces a high-accuracy digital replica of a human identity based on a recommended 1-3 hours of original human voice recordings.
Once generated, the audiobook clips were downsampled to 22050Hz, loudness-normalised (EBU R 128), and converted from WAV to MP3 for presentation within the online experiment.
The main willingness-to-wait task comprised 4 experimental trials (one per audiobook) presented in random order.

Of these trials, 2 featured a gender-congruent narration (e.g. a male-expected story read in a male-sounding voice) and 2 featured a gender-incongruent narration (e.g. a male-expected story read in a female-sounding voice).
The assignment of voice (Christopher or Elizabeth) to each story was counterbalanced across 4 versions of the experiment.

The experimental trials were interspersed with 2 vigilance trials in fixed positions (after the 1 st and 3 rd experimental trials), in which the participants were required to choose the number stated by a synthetic voice (1 female-sounding, 1 male-sounding; both distinct from the main trial narrator voices).

Participants recruited from Prolific were directed to the experiment on Gorilla Experiment Builder (Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020) where they read the study information sheet and provided informed consent.

text.text: Each participant was assigned to one of the 4 versions of the experiment.
Each experimental trial had the same structure (Figure 1): After presentation of a fixation cross, the participant heard the first spoken audio excerpt from a book lasting 30-40 seconds.
text.formatted: Each experimental trial had the same structure (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>): After presentation of a fixation cross, the participant heard the first spoken audio excerpt from a book lasting 30-40 seconds.

text.text: When the audio clip finished playing, the participant rated their enjoyment of the excerpt using a 9-point visual analogue scale (where1 = "hated it" and9 = "loved it").
The next screen presented a written comprehension question (as used by Jones et al., 2025), which the participant answered by selecting from 4 choices.
text.formatted: The next screen presented a written comprehension question (as used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Jones et al., 2025)</ref>, which the participant answered by selecting from 4 choices.

text.text: Next, the participant indicated whether they had heard or read the book before.
Finally, the participant was asked if they would like to wait to hear some more of the book.
If they chose to wait, the second audio excerpt would play following a delay of 4.5 seconds (with participants having the option to move on to the next trial at any point during this second clip).
If they chose to skip, the next trial began after 500ms.
After all 4 trials, participants were presented again with the first excerpt from each of the 4 books.

Here, they were instructed to rate how suitable they found the voice as a narrator for each of the excerpts, where suitability was further defined as whether the narrator's voice was a good fit to the content of the excerpt.
Suitability was rated from 0-100, where0 = not at all suitable and100 = extremely suitable.
To facilitate this decision, each audio narration was accompanied by the text of the excerpt onscreen.
Participants did not have to listen to the whole clip before making their rating.

After rating suitability for all 4 stories, the participants were asked which of the 2 narrator voices sounded more pleasant to them, with the response options "male voice", "female voice", and "no preference".
Participants were then invited to, if relevant, report any technical difficulties and make further comments about the experiment.

Finally, the participants were given the opportunity to recommend removal of their data from the analyses, without penalty, if they felt they had not completed the tasks properly (i.e. by following all the task instructions and engaging with the tasks attentively).

Data were analysed with (generalised) linear mixed models in RStudio with lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), using the afex package (Singmann et al., 2016) to estimate main effects via likelihood ratio tests.

text.text: Initial random-effects structures were maximal, with effects removed in the presence of convergence failures, singular fits, and/or boundary solutions.
Models used a binomial error distribution and logit link function to model binary response outcomes.
Full model tables (prepared using lme4 and sjPlot) were used to report estimates / odds ratios and their 95% confidence intervals.
Categorical predictors were coded using sum (deviation) contrasts.
Ratings of Enjoyment and suitability (henceforth Fit) were coded as numerical variables.
Responses to the Comprehension questions were scored as 1 (correct) or 0 (incorrect).
Waiting was coded as 1 (wait) or 0 (skip).

The Enjoyment and Fit variables were mean-centred across participants for inclusion in mixed models, and all trials where the participant reported having previously heard or read the book were also removed (7 trials in total, from 7 unique participants).

The first family of models tested the effect of gender congruence (congruent vs incongruent) on enjoyment (1), the likelihood of answering the comprehension question accurately (2), and the likelihood of waiting to hear more of the spoken narrative (3).
A further model was run to validate the experimental manipulation by using participants' post-hoc Fit ratings:
Finally, a series of exploratory models was run to support further understanding of the results.
The first model tested whether, as shown in previous work (Bains et al., 2023; Jones et al., 2025; McGettigan et al., 2026), enjoyment of the narrative was significantly predictive of waiting.

text.text: The remaining models tested the effect of post-hoc Fit ratings as predictors of Enjoyment, Accuracy, and Waiting in the main experiment.

Here, two predictor variables were constructed: Fit_consensus represented the mean ratings of Fit per unique book and condition combination (i.e. 8 values in total), and Fit_individual represented the participant's trialwise deviation from that mean.

In the model tables, the estimated effect sizes reflect the deviation of each condition from the grand mean: For ease of interpretation, the effect sizes for the contrast of gender-congruent vs. gender-incongruent conditions were therefore computed as 2β for linear mixed-effects models and as exp(2β) for the logistic mixed-effects models.
The mean enjoyment rating of the initial book excerpts was 5.60 (out of 9; SD = 1.27) for gender-congruent narrations and 5.55 (SD = 1.24) for gender-incongruent narrations.
Mean comprehension accuracy was 75.9% for gender-congruent narrations and 76.5% for genderincongruent narrations.

Participants waited to hear more of the book on a total of 155 trials for the gender-congruent narrations and 108 trials for the gender-incongruent narrations; this corresponded to mean waiting rates of 19.6% and 13.8%, respectively.
Mean post-hoc ratings of narrator-to-story Fit were 77.87 (out of 100; SD = 14.9) for gender-congruent narrations and 48.43 (SD = 23.4) for gender-incongruent narrations.

text.text: In the current experiment, listeners' enjoyment of a book was predictive of their motivation to continue listening to it, but at the same time only listening motivation was enhanced by greater gender congruency between the book's narration and its content.

This observation could be explained via the difference between the immediate experience of listening to each book's first excerpt and the motivational salience attached to the book on the basis of that excerpt: for incongruent stories, the violation of gender stereotypes may add some processing cost to the integration of the excerpt's meaning with the medium of delivery, for example via attempts to revise and repair what has been perceived (Lattner & Friederici, 2003; Porkert et al., 2024).

A more parsimonious explanation for the results could be that while the experimental manipulation of gender congruency alone was insufficient to modulate listeners' conscious experience of the spoken narrative, an alternative measure of overall narrator-to-story "fit" might be more effective in capturing variance in enjoyment.

The finding that individual "taste" in narrator-to-story fit significantly predicted both greater "liking" and "wanting" suggests that the relationship of the narrator to the book content can indeed shape both listeners' experience of a spoken narrative as well as its incentive salience to motivate continued listening.
Crucially, however, consensus on fit -like the overall gender congruency manipulation -only significantly predicted motivation.
This profile of findings raises the question of how the assignment of a narrator to a book might operate at scale.

On the one hand, the evidence that the "wisdom of the crowd" could be used to nudge behavioural decision-making and extend engagement with a book is an encouraging finding, as greater exposure to books is linked to greater benefits (Mol & Bus, 2011).

text.text: However, if the goal of narrator-to-story matching is enjoyment, given the power of perceived hedonistic pleasure to itself incentivise motivated behaviour, then the evidence presented here suggests that narrator assignment may require additional listener-specific considerations.
However, there are some important considerations that limit interpretability of the findings.

Here, listeners were exposed to a relatively small number of trials and, due to counterbalancing, the consensus ratings of fit were necessarily established based on subsets of participants who heard the same combinations of story and narrator rather than using the overall group consensus.

That neither the categorical gender congruence manipulation nor post-hoc fit ratings could predict comprehension may also reflect ceiling effects in the dependent variable, given two of the questions yielded mean accuracy scores exceeding 85%.

Thus, in order to better understand the predictive power of perceived narrator-to-story fit on listener experience and listening outcomes, and to test the robustness of the effects found in Experiment 1, it is necessary to investigate the impact of fit across a larger number of stories, independently of any additional experimental manipulation, and across truly independent listener groups.
This experiment focused on narrator-to-story fit as a continuous predictor of narrative listening experiences and outcomes.

Participants were given the opportunity to take a short a break after the 10 th story.

The current study presents two novel experiments investigating how the fit between the sound of a narrator and the content of the book being narrated influences the listener's experience and their behaviours in response to the story.

Overall, the findings show that while aspects of fit can significantly predict how much listeners enjoy and engage with a story, these effects are neither consistent across measures, nor across listener samples.

Specifically, while both a between-sample, consensus-derived categorical manipulation of narrator-to-story gender congruence as well as within-sample consensus ratings of narrator-to-story fit could significantly predict listeners' motivation to continue listening to a story, listening enjoyment was much more dependent on listener-specific impressions of fit.
Listening comprehension was consistently insensitive to any measure or manipulation of narrator-to-story fit.

A key outcome of the current findings is that enjoyment and waiting -or, "liking" and "wanting" (Berridge & Kringelbach, 2008) -were differentially sensitive to manipulated or rated variation in narrator-to-story fit.

text.text: While both ratings of enjoyment and the choice to continue engaging with a book were expressed as conscious decisions on the part of the listener, the latter was nonetheless sensitive to the "wisdom of the crowd".
In Experiment 1, the categorical manipulation of gender-congruence was determined based on an independent group of readers' ratings of the "ideal" narrator's gender.

The findings showed that pairing a book that gave those readers a strong expectation of a male or female narrator with an audio narration categorically matching that expectation was sufficient to increase engagement, via more frequent waiting decisions, in an independent group of listeners.

Similarly, consensus-based mean ratings of overall narrator-to-story fit collected from the group of listeners in Experiment 1 significantly predicted the same sample's waiting decisions in response to gender-congruent and gender-incongruent narrations.

Mechanistically, the dissociation between enjoyment and motivation in Experiment 1 suggests that categorical manipulations of gender congruence (and the related perception of narrator-to-story fit) do not operate directly on hedonistic pleasure responses but may otherwise affect the assignment of value to the book and, consequently, the strength of the incentive to continue listening.

This may come about due to the increased cognitive cost of integrating a narrative with an unexpected narrator (e.g. Lattner & Friederici, 2003), rather than due to an incongruent narration being less enjoyable per se.

text.text: However, it is important to note that the robustness of consensus data was limited in the current study, as Experiment 2 found that consensus ratings of narratorto-story fit for a larger set of 20 stories did not predict waiting decisions in a fully independent participant sample.
There are a number of possible reasons why effects did not generalise across these two samples.

First, the presence of two narrators in Experiment 1 may have been sufficiently more salient to engage listeners with narrator identity in the willingness-to-wait task than the single female-sounding narrator in Experiment 2.

Second, the gender congruence manipulation in Experiment 1 may have been more effective in modulating the ease of integration of information during listening, in line with previous findings of neural and behavioural sensitivities to apparent conflicts between the perceived gender of a speaker and the meaning of the spoken message (Casado et al., 2023; Lattner & Friederici, 2003; Porkert et al., 2024; Sommers & Danielson, 1999).

text.text: In conclusion, it is most likely that consensus estimates of narrator-to-story fit can be impactful on motivated behaviour when the range or contrast of fit is sufficiently salient to disrupt the integration of the voice and the spoken message.
In contrast to motivated behaviour, measures of listening enjoyment showed a much greater dependence on the individual listener's evaluation of the narrator-to-story fit.

Specifically, participant-specific trialwise deviations from mean fit ratings were significantly able to predict trial-specific ratings of story enjoyment in both Experiment 1 and Experiment 2: when a participant rated a narrative higher than the aggregate rating, they enjoyed it more.
In contrast, the aggregate (or consensus) rating was independently unable to predict within-sample enjoyment, in either experiment.
This is a clear demonstration of the importance of personal taste in shaping the experience of narrative listening.

The finding aligns with our previous findings that listeners enjoy narratives more, and are more willing to continue listening, when they are narrated in voices that are personally familiar to them (i.e. their own voice, the voice of a friend; McGettigan et al., 2026) -personally-familiar and personally-valued voices have separately been shown to implicate reward-related brain circuitry (Abrams et al., 2016 (Abrams et al., , 2019 (Abrams et al., , 2022;; Kanber et al., 2025) and motivated behaviour in comparison with less valued familiar and unfamiliar voices (Kanber et al., 2025).

text.text: Taken together, our current findings and those of relevant previous studies emphasise the personal nature of affective and hedonistic experience when listening to voices.

If enjoyment is a crucial lever with which to promote engagement with narrative listening, these findings in turn suggest the potential importance of personalising the listening experience, to yield gains in engagement via boosts in enjoyment.
However, it is not the case that enjoyment is completely insensitive to consensus-based intervention.

text.text: The experience of a pleasant or attractive voice may therefore hold some level of intrinsic value that can generalise across listeners.

In the context of narrative listening, the simple effect of vocal pleasantness on enjoyment may also explain the observation that some audiobook listeners will even tolerate listening to poor quality books simply because of their love of the narrator (Spjeldnæs & Karlsen, 2024).

text.text: Our findings further contribute to developing theoretical accounts of narrative listening.

The Model of Listening Engagement (MoLE) considers the interplay of engagement (recruitment of resources), motivation (willingness to recruit those resources), and experiences (enjoyment, boredom, effort) in narrative listening (Herrmann & Johnsrude, 2020).
text.formatted: The Model of Listening Engagement (MoLE) considers the interplay of engagement (recruitment of resources), motivation (willingness to recruit those resources), and experiences (enjoyment, boredom, effort) in narrative listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Herrmann & Johnsrude, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The MoLE posits that listening motivation can influence both engagement and experiences, while experiences can only directly modulate motivation (and not engagement).

Our core willingness-to-wait measures repeatedly align with this proposal: increased situational enjoyment of a narrative significantly predicted the decision to wait in Experiment 1 of the current paper, and in all three experiments of McGettigan et al. (2026).

(2026)</ref>.

text.text: Our further findings in relation to both narrator voice identity and its relationship to the narrative's content then suggest how the properties of a narrative itself -i.e. qualities external to the listener -can shape this underlying mechanism.

Here, it is perhaps of greatest relevance to the development of the model that adjustments to narrative voice identity can dissociate in their impacts on listening experiences (here, enjoyment) and motivation (here, the willingness to continue listening).
The current study immediately presents several pathways for further investigation.
One unresolved question is the degree to which narrator-to-story fit "breaks through" into the situational listening experience.

On the one hand, our findings show that a relatively drastic categorical manipulation of gender congruency yielded variation in perceived narrator fit sufficient to impact enjoyment and engagement (Experiment 1) but this did not replicate to a wider story set and different narrator-story pairing (Experiment 2).
Future work should explore whether a wider range of aggregate estimates of fit would indeed continuously predict independent listeners' enjoyment and engagement across a larger number of narratives.

Another dimension worth exploring is the degree to which the listener's experience of narratorto-story fit might depend on their explicit consideration of fit during situational listening: In Experiment 2, listeners were aware that they should rate both enjoyment and fit per trial, and therefore may have paid greater attention to fit as a component of their enjoyment.

Although this cannot explain the dissociation between individual and consensus fit ratings within that same experiment, it would be beneficial to compare the within-group findings from Experiment 2 to an experiment in which participants first listen to and rate all stories for enjoyment and then separately consider narrator-to-story fit.
However, these relationships between perceived fit and experienced enjoyment and engagement would still be estimated retroactively.

An altogether more suitable approach, and one that may lend itself more cleanly to application, would be to examine narrator-to-story fit in the context of allowing listeners to proactively choose or design a narrator for their narrative listening experience. Bains et al. (2025) found that offering readers a choice of book title or genre was sufficient to significantly boost their situational enjoyment of the chosen book's synopsis, compared with having no choice.

text.text: This may be related to increased agency over the experience, which could also apply to having a choice of narrator voice -for example, previous work has shown that choosing a voice to represent the self is associated with stronger perceptual prioritisation of that voice compared with being assigned a self-voice (Payne et al., 2021).

text.text: However, the act of choosing (or designing) a narrator also allows the listener to freely and non-prescriptively consider their individual needs and preferences in relation to the listening experience.

This could include the fit between the perceived narrator and the book genre or sample content, and/or more global considerations of what sound "good" in terms of voice attractiveness or other perceived attributes like masculinity or accent.

We predict that offering listeners the opportunity to choose a narrator should increase enjoyment, with concomitant boosts to comprehension and waiting, compared with having no choice -within this, there would then be opportunities to determine whether listener choices that boost enjoyment map well onto individual or aggregate estimates of concepts including narrator-to-story fit.
